note: The rubric for judging which programming language fits a system (EE-189). Each criterion's weight is an unvalidated prior: nobody has measured that these weights pick better languages, and a person may set others for a system. A gate criterion rules out a candidate scored 0 on it. A score never decides: packages/naive/src/engine/language-rubric.ts ranks the candidates and a person chooses. The worked examples record Naive's own choices; their scores are a rater's judgment from the cited decisions and files, and the choices are the decisions'.

criteria.title: Fit to the runtime target
criteria.question: Does the language run where the system must run: a browser, an edge worker, a server, a device or a build in CI?
criteria.why: A language that cannot run on the target needs a second system to host it, and that is a different choice. Browsers run JavaScript and WebAssembly, and Node.js runs TypeScript only by stripping erasable syntax and refuses TypeScript files under node_modules, so even one language can fit one target and not another.

levels.means: It cannot run on the target.
It runs there through a compile step, WebAssembly or a bridge, with gaps the system must work around.
It runs there after a build step with no gaps.
It runs there as written, as the target's documented language.

criteria.title: Correctness needs
criteria.question: How well does the language catch the errors this system cannot afford: by tests only, by static types, or by machine-checked proof?
criteria.why: Some systems only need tests, some need types that rule out whole classes of error, and some must prove a property. TypeScript does not aim for a sound type system by design; Lean checks proofs in dependent type theory, which is where Naive proves its definitions.

levels.means: No static checking of what the system needs; errors show up only when the code runs.
Optional static checks bolted on (comments or annotations a checker reads).
Static types that catch shape errors, unsound by design.
A sound static type system for the properties the system needs.
Machine-checked proofs of the properties the system needs.

criteria.title: Concurrency and effect model
criteria.question: Can code in the language say what may fail, what touches files or services and what runs at the same time, so a test can replace it?
criteria.why: Naive's code that reads or writes files, can fail or runs work at once is written as Effects: failures are typed, files are reached through a service a test swaps for an in-memory one. A language without such a model leaves those facts to convention.

levels.means: No way to run work concurrently, or to tell a failure from a result.
Exceptions and callbacks or promises; failures are not in any signature.
Structured concurrency or typed errors, but not both, or only by convention.
Failures, dependencies and concurrency are in the types, and a test can provide a replacement service.

criteria.title: Ecosystem and libraries for the domain
criteria.question: Does the system's domain have maintained, documented libraries in this language for what the system must do?
criteria.why: A missing library is code the venture writes and keeps. Count only libraries a person can name and read; do not score from popularity surveys or download counts.

levels.means: Nothing for the domain; the system would write it all.
Libraries exist for part of the domain, or are thinly maintained.
Maintained, documented libraries cover what the system must do.

criteria.title: Interop with Naive
criteria.question: How directly can the system read and write Naive's records, which are JSON validated by JSON Schema, and call the router, which is TypeScript?
criteria.why: Every write in a venture meets the gate and provenance through the router. A system that reaches records only through a hand-written bridge can drift from the schemas the router checks.

levels.means: Neither JSON records nor the router are reachable without a hand-written bridge.
It reads and validates JSON records against their schemas, and reaches the router only through the CLI, the MCP server or the HTTP API.
It imports the router in process, without types for the records.
It imports the router and the record types generated from the schemas in process.

criteria.title: Team skill
criteria.question: Can the people and agents who will keep the system read and change code in this language today?
criteria.why: Code nobody on the team can change is a system the team cannot keep. EE-087 chose TypeScript for Naive's own development and left founders the choice for their ventures, because many have never coded.

levels.means: Nobody who will keep the system reads the language.
Someone reads it, but changes need outside help or long review.
The people and agents who keep the system already write it.

criteria.title: Operability
criteria.question: How much does it take to build, install, deploy, observe and debug the system on its target in this language?
criteria.why: A build step, a toolchain to install or a package format the target refuses is work on every release. Naive compiles on publish because Node.js will not strip types under node_modules.

levels.means: No supported way to build or run it on the target.
A toolchain to install and a build with its own failure modes on every release.
One build step the repository runs for you.
It runs as written, with nothing to build or install beyond the runtime.

criteria.title: Licence
criteria.question: Do the language's toolchain and the libraries the system needs carry licences the venture may use and ship under?
criteria.why: A licence that forbids the use rules a language out whatever it scores elsewhere; a copyleft licence on shipped code is an obligation to track. ISO/IEC 25010 does not cover licences, so the SPDX License List is the reference for which licence is which.

levels.means: A licence forbids the use the venture needs.
Permitted, with obligations to track (copyleft on shipped code, attribution beyond a notice).
Permissive OSI-approved licences, such as MIT or Apache-2.0.

examples.system: Naive's framework code: the records resolver, the router, the engine, the checks and the CLIs, installed into a venture as the naive-framework package.
examples.target: server: Node.js 22.19 or later, in the repository and from node_modules

why.runtime-fit: Node.js runs the source by type stripping in the repository, but refuses TypeScript under node_modules, so the package ships compiled .mjs in dist/ (EE-159, nodejs-typescript-docs).
why.correctness: Static types, with every record type generated from its JSON Schema (EE-087); TypeScript is not sound by design (typescript-design-goals).
why.effects-and-concurrency: Effect puts failures in the signature as tagged errors and reaches files through VentureFs, which a test replaces with MemoryFs (EE-125, effect-docs).
why.ecosystem: The npm registry; Naive's own dependencies, effect and typescript, are npm packages.
why.naive-interop: The router is TypeScript and the record types are generated into packages/naive/src/records/types/records.d.ts, imported in process (EE-087).
why.team-skill: The founder chose TypeScript for Naive's own development (EE-087), and every new file in the repository is .ts.
why.operability: One build step, scripts/build.ts, run by npm as prepare (EE-159), and a Node.js floor of 22.19 (EE-158).
why.licence: TypeScript is Apache-2.0 and Effect is MIT (spdx-license-list).

why.runtime-fit: Node.js runs .mjs as written, from the repository and from node_modules.
why.correctness: Only what tsc reads with allowJs and checkJs, EE-087's first phase.
why.effects-and-concurrency: Promises and exceptions; failures are in no signature.
why.naive-interop: It imports the router in process, without the generated record types.
why.team-skill: Naive was written in JavaScript before EE-087, so the code and the agents already read it.
why.licence: Node.js and the npm packages Naive uses carry permissive licences; no extra toolchain.

rated.basis: The cited decisions and the repository's AGENTS.md; a person may change any score.

examples.note: EE-087 also keeps Rust for later hot paths, called from TypeScript. No hot path has been named, so Rust is not scored here.

examples.system: The proofs that settle Naive's definitions (packages/naive/lean/Naive), whose theorem names the term engine checks (EE-095).
examples.target: a build in CI (lake build in the lean workflow)

why.runtime-fit: The proofs only need to build, and CI builds them with lake (packages/naive/lean/README.md).
why.correctness: Lean checks proofs in a dependent type theory powerful enough for almost any conventional mathematical theorem (lean-theorem-proving).
why.ecosystem: Core Lean for most files; Mathlib for the real square roots and logarithms in StandingRules.lean (packages/naive/lean/README.md).
why.naive-interop: No in-process calls: lean-agreement-test.ts reads the .lean files and ties the term engine's theorem names to them.
why.team-skill: Naive already keeps its proofs in Lean, and its conventions follow spct-lean (packages/naive/lean/README.md).
why.operability: A pinned toolchain installed with elan, and a Mathlib cache to download before lake build.

why.runtime-fit: It builds and runs in CI like the rest of Naive.
why.correctness: Not sound by design (typescript-design-goals), so its types prove nothing; below the system's must of 4.
why.ecosystem: Naive's term engine checks properties on facts in TypeScript as tests (EE-095); it asks Lean for the proofs.
why.naive-interop: The term engine and the router are TypeScript.
why.team-skill: Every new file in the repository is .ts.
why.operability: The same build step as the framework.

rated.basis: EE-095, packages/naive/lean/README.md and the cited references; a person may change any score.

examples.note: The effect model does not apply to proofs, so its weight is 0 for this system and it is not scored.
